title: From Rows to Reasoning: A Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Framework for Spreadsheet Understanding

problem.claim: Large language models struggle to reason over large-scale enterprise spreadsheets with many numeric rows, linked sheets, and embedded visual content.

gap.claim: Existing spreadsheet reasoning approaches rely mainly on single-sheet compression or full-context encoding, limiting scalability and failing to reflect interaction with complex multimodal workbooks.

contributions.claim: FRTR-Bench is a large-scale benchmark for multimodal spreadsheet reasoning, containing 30 enterprise-grade Excel workbooks, nearly four million cells, and more than 50 embedded images.

FRTR is a multimodal retrieval-augmented generation framework that decomposes workbooks into row, column, and block embeddings, combines lexical-dense retrieval with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and uses multimodal embeddings for numerical and visual information.

author_reported_evidence.claim: FRTR was tested on six LLMs and achieved 74% answer accuracy on FRTR-Bench with Claude Sonnet 4.5.
On enterprise-scale, multi-sheet workbooks in FRTR-Bench, FRTR reportedly improved over the best existing baseline by 50 percentage points, from 24% to 74%.

On the single-sheet SpreadsheetLLM benchmark, FRTR reportedly achieved 87% accuracy with GPT-5 versus 90% for SpreadsheetLLM while reducing token usage by roughly 50% compared with direct serialization methods.

narrative_sequence.summary: Large enterprise spreadsheets create reasoning challenges because of their scale, linked sheets, and visual content.
Prior approaches do not scale well and inadequately represent real interaction with multimodal workbooks.
The work introduces FRTR-Bench and the FRTR retrieval-augmented multimodal framework.
The authors report results across six LLMs and both enterprise-scale multi-sheet and single-sheet benchmarks.

source_observation.claim: The framework retrieves granular row, column, and block representations and combines lexical, dense, and multimodal signals for spreadsheet reasoning.

interpretation.claim: For complex multimodal documents, structured decomposition and hybrid retrieval may improve access to relevant evidence while avoiding full-context encoding.

application.claim: A document-question-answering system could combine fine-grained structural indexing with lexical-dense and visual retrieval.

exception.claim: The reported single-sheet result was below the comparison system's accuracy, despite lower token usage.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the six evaluated LLMs beyond Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5.
The abstract does not describe dataset construction, evaluation protocols, statistical variation, or failure cases.
